This was done so that the matters raised by the Court's opinion could be dealt with in the instant rulemaking proceeding, which has a much more current record and is in its final stage. Furthermore, many of the Court's observations are of particular interest in this proceeding, for although the Court had only the specific issue of freight forwarder terminal areas before it, its comments are germane to the proper administration and interpretation of both section 202(c) and section 203 (b)(8). Consequently, we have endeavored to keep the Court's directives before us in our evaluation of the evidence of record and our formulation of the proper geographic limits of the exemptions provided by sections 202(c) and 203(b)(8).
The freight forwarders assert that the National Transportation Policy requires that forwarding be fostered, for otherwise it is impossible for small shipments to move in linehaul, terminal-to-terminal service by the energyefficient rail mode. We agree that a healthy freight forwarding industry is in the public interest, and we adhere to the findings of the Interim Report that expansion of freight forwarder terminal areas should lead to increased efficiency and other benefits, Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 172. In light of our conclusions in this proceeding with respect to the modern limits of commercial zones and motor carrier terminal areas, we believe that the freight forwarders should share in the expanded geographic scope of the exemption provided by section 202(c). The critical issue is whether freight forwarder and motor carrier terminal areas should continue to encompass identical areas.
